title: Track 1, Lesson 6: Paying off debt sensibly - Snowball vs Avalanche
subtitle: Two different repayment strategies - one optimises the money, the other the motivation. Pick the one that fits the person you actually are.
whyItMatters: Getting the repayment order right can save you millions in interest, or stop you giving up halfway through for lack of momentum. This lesson gives you both options and how to choose between them.
openingQuestion: You have 3 debts: a credit card of 10m (30% a year), a consumer loan of 30m (15% a year), and a car on finance at 50m (8% a year). Under the Avalanche method, which do you pay first?
openingOptions: The 30m consumer loan, as the middle amount
The 10m credit card, because it carries the highest rate (30% a year)
The 50m car finance, because it is the largest balance of the three debts
All three equally at the same time
explanation: There are two ways to order repayments. The avalanche puts spare money into the highest-rate debt first, and it is optimal arithmetically - the least total interest paid. The snowball clears the smallest balance first; it costs more but gives an early sense of winning, so many people stay with it longer. Because the hard part of paying off debt is sustaining it over several years, the method that is optimal on paper is not always optimal in practice.

diagram.label: Choose by the person you actually are

realWorldExample.description: Someone using Avalanche clears the 30%-a-year credit card first and saves the most interest over time. But many people in practice choose Snowball (smallest balance first, whatever the rate) because the feeling of "wiping out" a debt creates the momentum to keep the discipline going for longer.

quiz.question: In what order does the Snowball method pay debts?
options: Splitting the payment evenly across every debt
By highest interest rate first, whatever the balance
In the order the debts were originally taken on
By smallest balance first, whatever the interest rate
quiz.explanation: Snowball clears the SMALLEST BALANCE first, regardless of rate. It is less optimal than Avalanche arithmetically, but psychologically, wiping out a debt quickly creates a sense of success that helps many people keep paying for longer.

quiz.question: When should you pick Snowball over Avalanche, even though Avalanche saves more interest?
options: When you tend to give up and need a run of small wins
When you want to minimise the interest you pay
When every debt you hold happens to carry the same rate
When the largest debt also carries the highest rate
quiz.explanation: Both methods are reasonable depending on the person: Avalanche optimises the arithmetic, Snowball optimises the behaviour. If you have abandoned a financial plan halfway before, Snowball may be the more realistic choice even though it costs a little more in theory.

quiz.question: You have debt A (5m at 20%), debt B (40m at 25%), debt C (8m at 10%). What order does Avalanche give? And Snowball?
options: Avalanche: A→B→C | Snowball: C→B→A
Avalanche: B→A→C | Snowball: A→C→B
Avalanche and Snowball always give the same order
Avalanche: C→A→B | Snowball: B→A→C
quiz.explanation: Avalanche runs down the rates: B (25%) → A (20%) → C (10%). Snowball runs up the balances: A (5m) → C (8m) → B (40m). The two give completely different orders because the sorting criterion is different - one by rate, the other by amount.

quiz.question: Debt A of 5 million at 20%, debt B of 40 million at 25%, debt C of 8 million at 10%. What order does Snowball give?
options: C → A → B (by rising interest rate, which is neither method)
B → A → C (by falling interest rate, which is Avalanche)
A → C → B (by balance, from smallest to largest)
A → B → C (by the debts' labels rather than by balance)
quiz.explanation: Snowball sorts by balance regardless of rate: 5 million → 8 million → 40 million. Clearing A within a few months gives a visible win, and that feeling is what keeps people going - even though Avalanche (B → A → C) saves more interest.

quiz.question: What do Snowball and Avalanche both require?
options: Negotiating the rate down before starting to repay anything
Splitting any spare money evenly across all the debts you hold
Stopping payments on everything else until the target is cleared
Paying the minimum on everything, and the surplus into one debt
quiz.explanation: The two methods differ only in which debt is the target; the mechanism is identical. Splitting spare money evenly means nothing gets cleared early, and stopping other payments triggers penalty fees and damages your credit history.

keyTakeaways: Avalanche (highest rate → lowest) optimises the money; Snowball (smallest balance → largest) optimises the motivation - choose by the person you actually are
Both methods require the same thing: pay the minimum on everything else, put the surplus into the target debt
The best method is the one you genuinely see through to the end, not the one that is optimal on paper

practicePrompt.question: You have 4 small debts and one large low-rate debt. You have abandoned a repayment plan halfway before, because it felt like 'no progress was happening'. Which method fits that trait better?
options: Snowball - clear the smallest debts first whatever the rate, to create a sense of winning and keep the momentum
Avalanche - pay the highest-rate debt first, since this is always the financially optimal choice regardless of any personal psychological trait
Neither method suits, so pay every debt equally each month for the sake of fairness across all of them
It makes no difference which method you choose, because the end result always turns out the same whichever one you apply
practicePrompt.explanation: The best method is the one you genuinely see through - for someone who tends to give up, Snowball's run of small wins sustains momentum better than Avalanche.

summary.keyIdea: Avalanche (highest rate → lowest) optimises the money; Snowball (smallest balance → largest) optimises the motivation - choose by the person you actually are
summary.commonMistake: Reading the idea as a phrase to remember rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.
summary.action: Both methods require the same thing: pay the minimum on everything else, put the surplus into the target debt

application.title: Make the list
application.message: Write down every debt you hold with its rate and balance, then sort it both ways - avalanche (highest rate first) and snowball (smallest balance first) - and see which order you would genuinely stick to.
application.secondary: The best method is the one you can see through to the end.

sections.text: With several debts at once, the question is not only "which do I pay first" but "which method will I actually see through". Snowball and Avalanche are the two most common strategies - one optimises the money saved, the other the psychological momentum. There is no absolute right answer, only the one that fits the person you actually are.

Avalanche targets the debt with the HIGHEST INTEREST RATE first - every spare dong goes there, while everything else gets only the minimum. Once the highest-rate debt is cleared you move to the second highest, and so on. This is arithmetically optimal: the total interest you pay across the whole process is as low as it can be.

Snowball targets the SMALLEST BALANCE first, whatever the rate. Arithmetically it is less efficient than Avalanche - you may pay some unnecessary interest. But psychologically, wiping out a debt quickly creates a sense of victory that helps many people hold the discipline for longer - especially if you have abandoned financial plans halfway in the past.

left.label: Avalanche
left.text: Pay by rate, high → low. Saves the most interest. Suits disciplined people who don't need small wins to keep going.

right.label: Snowball
right.text: Pay by balance, small → large. Creates a quick sense of victory. Suits people who lose heart easily and need visible progress.

sections.text: **Example:** debt A (5 million at 20%), debt B (40 million at 25%), debt C (8 million at 10%). Avalanche pays in the order B → A → C (rates falling). Snowball pays A → C → B (balances rising). The two give completely different orders because they sort on different criteria.

items: Both methods require the same thing: pay the minimum on every other debt, and put all the surplus into the target
Choose Avalanche if you trust your own discipline and want to save the most interest
Choose Snowball if you know you lose heart easily and need a run of small wins to keep going
Whichever you choose, take on no new debt while you are clearing the old

lines: The best method is not the one that is optimal on paper, but the one you actually carry through to the end.
